journeys.title: The American BBQ Belt by train
journeys.dek: Vinegar, mustard, white sauce, and post oak, from eastern North Carolina to South Texas.
intro: This train does not pretend the South has one barbecue. It stops where the wood, the animal, and the sauce actually change.

Eastern North Carolina chops a whole hog with vinegar and pepper. Lexington reddens a shoulder dip with a little tomato. The South Carolina Midlands reach for mustard. Alabama’s white sauce is mayonnaise. Memphis leaves the ribs dry. Owensboro cooks mutton. St. Louis and Chicago cut the shoulder into steaks and tips. Kansas City cubes the brisket point. Texas, at the end of the line, salts beef and, in the south of the state, pits a head.
The leg is by train because that is how these regions once sat on the same map of rails, markets, and moving cooks. It is a reading route, not a timetable.

intro: These fires moved by sea. Sour orange and garlic in Cuba, allspice and scotch bonnet in Jamaica, a boucan in Haiti, wasakaka in the Dominican Republic, lechón in Puerto Rico, chadon beni in Trinidad, flying fish in Barbados.
The boat is the vehicle because that is how pigs, chile, and citrus actually traveled. Each stop is its own kitchen.

journeys.title: Asado and churrasco by plane
journeys.dek: A flight across the southern fires, from the parrilla to picanha.
intro: The distance from a Buenos Aires parrilla to a Brazilian picanha skewer is a plane ride, not a stroll. The fire idea is shared. The cuts are not.

This route starts with an Argentine asado, crosses the Río de la Plata, looks south to a Patagonian lamb, steps into a Chilean asado, and ends on Brazilian picanha. It is not a ranking of who grills better.

journeys.dek: A low pass over sardines, calçots, vine shoots, and a spit.
intro: A balloon is the right speed for this coast. The fire changes with the harbor: sardines on a Malaga beach, spring onions in Catalonia, lamb chops over Rioja vine cuttings, June sardines in Lisbon, an Easter lamb in Greece, a hand-minced kebab in Adana.
Nothing here is a fast transfer. The point is how close these shores are, and how different the grills still are.

journeys.title: Africa's fires by plane
journeys.dek: Mechoui, dibi, suya, nyama choma, and a braai.
intro: Africa does not have one grill. This flight is a way to taste how far the fires sit from each other: a Moroccan celebration lamb, a Dakar street dibi, Hausa suya, a Ghanaian tilapia, Kenyan nyama choma, Mozambican peri-peri chicken, and a South African braai sausage.
The plane is honest about the distance. It is not a claim that one coast taught the others.

journeys.title: Pacific earth ovens by boat
journeys.dek: Imu, lovo, umu, and hāngi. Related heat, separate peoples.
intro: An earth oven holds heat in the ground. Hawaiʻi, Fiji, Samoa, Tonga, and Aotearoa use that idea under different names, with different foods and different obligations.
The boat is the old way between these islands. A home pot in this journal is labeled as a home pot. It is not an imu, a lovo, an umu, or a marae hāngi.

intro: This is a long flight on purpose. Xinjiang lamb skewers, a Beijing duck, Cantonese char siu, Korean galbi, yakitori, Isaan grilled chicken, Malaysian satay, and a Cebu lechón do not belong to one cuisine.
The plane is just how a reader covers that distance. Each stop keeps its own wood, sugar, and rule for doneness.

books.title: Flying BBQ: The Top 100 Barbecue Dishes of the World
books.dek: A reading route through a hundred live-fire dishes chosen for reach and usefulness, not a prize list.
intro: These hundred stops are a route, not a contest. Each one is already in the passport. Nothing was invented to fill a slot.

They were chosen because a cook meets them far from home, or because they teach a method: a pit, a skewer, a spit, a tandoor, an earth oven. The order is a flight plan. Another editor would pack a different hundred.
The number of continents is counted from this list. It is not set in advance.

books.title: Appalachian Smoke
books.dek: Hickory shoulder, sorghum chops, a bought country-ham steak, and the pots that sit beside them.
intro: Appalachian stops in this book are the ones that can be tied to a real smoke or a real pot: hickory shoulder, sorghum-glazed chops, ramp-season trout, a purchased country-ham steak, vinegar chicken, a holiday turkey, chow-chow, soup beans, and skillet cornbread.

Scots-Irish and English settlers brought pork and vinegar habits into the mountains. German-speaking families brought sweet-sour pickling. Black Appalachian cooks worked the same farms and kitchens. Cherokee and other Native nations of these mountains had their own fire and corn long before those settlements. This book does not hand them a modern pulled-pork recipe.
Country ham here is a cured product you buy. The page cooks a steak of it. It does not teach home curing.

passages.title: Appalachian Smoke
passages.text: Scots-Irish and English settlers brought pork and vinegar habits into the mountains. German-speaking families brought sweet-sour pickling. Black Appalachian cooks worked the same farms and kitchens. Cherokee and other Native nations of these mountains had their own fire and corn long before those settlements. This book does not hand them a modern pulled-pork recipe.
passages.label: From the book

passages.title: Across the American South
passages.text: Enslaved cooks and their descendants built much of this public food. English, Scots-Irish, German, and Mexican traditions sit in particular places. The essays on each stop say which is which.

passages.title: Africa's Fires
passages.text: Where a dish was shaped by enslaved people, the page says so in plain language. Where it is a street grill or a feast, it says that instead.
